questions.solution:
Substitute $x^3 = \cos 2\theta$.

Then $\sqrt{1+x^3} = \sqrt{1+\cos 2\theta} = \sqrt{2}\cos\theta$

And $\sqrt{1-x^3} = \sqrt{1-\cos 2\theta} = \sqrt{2}\sin\theta$

$y = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}\cos\theta + \sqrt{2}\sin\theta}{\sqrt{2}\cos\theta - \sqrt{2}\sin\theta}\right)$

$y = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\cos\theta + \sin\theta}{\cos\theta - \sin\theta}\right)$

Dividing the numerator and denominator by $\cos\theta$:

$y = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1 + \tan\theta}{1 - \tan\theta}\right)$

$y = \tan^{-1}\left(\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} + \theta\right)\right)$

$y = \dfrac{\pi}{4} + \theta$

Since $x^3 = \cos 2\theta$, we have $\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}\cos^{-1}(x^3)$.

$y = \dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{1}{2}\cos^{-1}(x^3)$

Differentiating with respect to $x$:

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{2} \left( -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - (x^3)^2}} \right) \cdot \dfrac{d}{dx}(x^3)$

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{3x^2}{2\sqrt{1 - x^6}}$

Answer: $-\dfrac{3x^2}{2\sqrt{1-x^6}}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $X = \tan^{-1}\left[2\cos\left(2\sin^{-1}\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\right] + \cos^{-1}\left[\cos\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right)\right]$ and $Y = \sin^{-1}\left[\sin\left(\dfrac{11\pi}{6}\right)\right] + \tan^{-1}\left[\tan\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right)\right]$ then the value of $2X - Y$ is:
questions.solution:
Evaluating the first expression $X$:

$\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$

$\tan^{-1}\left[2\cos\left(2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right)\right] = \tan^{-1}\left[2\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\right] = \tan^{-1}\left(2\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\right) = \tan^{-1}(1) = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$

For the second term of $X$, the principal value branch of $\cos^{-1}$ is $[0, \pi]$:

$\cos^{-1}\left[\cos\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right)\right] = \cos^{-1}\left[\cos\left(2\pi - \dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)\right] = \cos^{-1}\left[\cos\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)\right] = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$

Thus, $X = \dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{5\pi}{6} = \dfrac{13\pi}{12}$

Evaluating the second expression $Y$:

The principal value branch of $\sin^{-1}$ is $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$:

$\sin^{-1}\left[\sin\left(\dfrac{11\pi}{6}\right)\right] = \sin^{-1}\left[\sin\left(2\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right] = \sin^{-1}\left[-\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right] = -\dfrac{\pi}{6}$

The principal value branch of $\tan^{-1}$ is $\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$:

$\tan^{-1}\left[\tan\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right)\right] = \tan^{-1}\left[\tan\left(\pi + \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\right] = \tan^{-1}\left[\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\right] = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$

Thus, $Y = -\dfrac{\pi}{6} + \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$

Calculating $2X - Y$:

$2X - Y = 2\left(\dfrac{13\pi}{12}\right) - \dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{13\pi}{6} - \dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{12\pi}{6} = 2\pi$

Answer: $2\pi$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The value of the expression $\cos^{-1}\left(\cos\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right) + \sin^{-1}\left(\sin\dfrac{22\pi}{3}\right) + \tan^{-1}\left(\tan\dfrac{4\pi}{5}\right)$ is:
questions.solution:
The principal value branch of $\cos^{-1}x$ is $[0, \pi]$.

$\cos^{-1}\left(\cos\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right) = \cos^{-1}\left(\cos\left(2\pi - \dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)\right) = \cos^{-1}\left(\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right) = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$

The principal value branch of $\sin^{-1}x$ is $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$.

$\sin^{-1}\left(\sin\dfrac{22\pi}{3}\right) = \sin^{-1}\left(\sin\left(7\pi + \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\right) = \sin^{-1}\left(-\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = -\dfrac{\pi}{3}$

The principal value branch of $\tan^{-1}x$ is $\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$.

$\tan^{-1}\left(\tan\dfrac{4\pi}{5}\right) = \tan^{-1}\left(\tan\left(\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{5}\right)\right) = \tan^{-1}\left(-\tan\dfrac{\pi}{5}\right) = -\dfrac{\pi}{5}$

Adding the three values:

$\dfrac{5\pi}{6} - \dfrac{\pi}{3} - \dfrac{\pi}{5} = \dfrac{25\pi - 10\pi - 6\pi}{30} = \dfrac{9\pi}{30} = \dfrac{3\pi}{10}$

Answer: $\dfrac{3\pi}{10}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: Which of the following is the simplest form of the expression $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{1+x^2} - 1}{x}\right)$ where $x \neq 0$
questions.solution:
Let $x = \tan\theta$, where $\theta \in (-\pi/2, \pi/2)$ and $\theta \neq 0$.

Substituting $x = \tan\theta$ in the given expression:

$\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{1+\tan^2\theta} - 1}{\tan\theta}\right)$

$= \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sec\theta - 1}{\tan\theta}\right)$

$= \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} - 1}{\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}}\right)$

$= \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1 - \cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\right)$

Using the trigonometric identities $1 - \cos\theta = 2\sin^2(\theta/2)$ and $\sin\theta = 2\sin(\theta/2)\cos(\theta/2)$:

$= \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2\sin^2(\theta/2)}{2\sin(\theta/2)\cos(\theta/2)}\right)$

$= \tan^{-1}\left(\tan(\theta/2)\right)$

Since $\theta \in (-\pi/2, \pi/2)$, $\theta/2 \in (-\pi/4, \pi/4)$, which lies in the principal value branch of $\tan^{-1}$.

$= \dfrac{\theta}{2}$

Substituting back $\theta = \tan^{-1}x$:

$= \dfrac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}x$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}x$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: Given $\cos \left(\tan ^{-1} x\right)=\sin \left(\cot ^{-1} \dfrac{3}{4}\right)$, then the value of $x$ is
questions.solution:
Let $\theta = \tan^{-1} x$. Then $\tan \theta = x$. Since $\cos \theta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 + \tan^2 \theta}}$, we have $\cos(\tan^{-1} x) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 + x^2}}$.

Let $\phi = \cot^{-1} \dfrac{3}{4}$. Then $\cot \phi = \dfrac{3}{4}$, which implies $\tan \phi = \dfrac{4}{3}$.

Using the identity $\sin \phi = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 + \cot^2 \phi}}$, we have $\sin(\cot^{-1} \dfrac{3}{4}) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 + (3/4)^2}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 + 9/16}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{25/16}} = \dfrac{4}{5}$.

Equating the two expressions: $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 + x^2}} = \dfrac{4}{5}$.

Squaring both sides: $\dfrac{1}{1 + x^2} = \dfrac{16}{25}$.

Thus, $1 + x^2 = \dfrac{25}{16}$, which gives $x^2 = \dfrac{25}{16} - 1 = \dfrac{9}{16}$.

Taking the square root, $x = \dfrac{3}{4}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{3}{4}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
The range of the principal value branch of $\tan^{-1}(x)$ is $(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2})$.

Given the expression $\tan^{-1}(\tan \dfrac{7\pi}{6})$, we first simplify the argument of the inverse tangent function.

Since $\tan(\pi + \theta) = \tan \theta$, we have $\tan \dfrac{7\pi}{6} = \tan(\pi + \dfrac{\pi}{6}) = \tan \dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

Substituting this back into the expression, we get $\tan^{-1}(\tan \dfrac{\pi}{6})$.

Since $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ lies within the principal value branch $(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2})$, the expression simplifies to $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
The given expression is $\tan \left\{\cos ^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right\}$.

First, simplify the term inside the cosine inverse function: $\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$.

We know that $\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

Substituting this into the expression, we get $\tan \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$.

Calculating the value inside the tangent function: $\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{\pi}{2} = -\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

Therefore, the expression becomes $\tan \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$.

Since $\tan(-\theta) = -\tan(\theta)$, we have $\tan \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = -\tan \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = -1$.

Answer: $-1$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: $\sin ^{-1}(x-1)+\cos ^{-1}(x-3)+\tan ^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x}{2-x^2}\right)=\cos ^{-1} k+\pi$, then the value of ' $k$ ' is
questions.solution:
The domain of $\sin^{-1}(x-1)$ is $-1 \le x-1 \le 1$, which implies $0 \le x \le 2$.

The domain of $\cos^{-1}(x-3)$ is $-1 \le x-3 \le 1$, which implies $2 \le x \le 4$.

For the expression to be defined, $x$ must satisfy both conditions, so $x = 2$.

Substituting $x = 2$ into the given equation:

$\sin^{-1}(2-1) + \cos^{-1}(2-3) + \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2}{2-2^2}\right) = \cos^{-1} k + \pi$

$\sin^{-1}(1) + \cos^{-1}(-1) + \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2}{-2}\right) = \cos^{-1} k + \pi$

$\dfrac{\pi}{2} + \pi + \tan^{-1}(-1) = \cos^{-1} k + \pi$

$\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \cos^{-1} k$

$\dfrac{\pi}{4} = \cos^{-1} k$

$k = \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The range of $x$ for which the equation $\sin ^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2 x}{1+x^2}\right)=2 \tan ^{-1} x$ holds true
questions.solution:
The expression $\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2x}{1+x^2}\right)$ is defined for $\left|\dfrac{2x}{1+x^2}\right| \leq 1$, which implies $2|x| \leq 1+x^2$, or $(|x|-1)^2 \geq 0$, which is true for all $x \in R$.

Recall the identity $\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2x}{1+x^2}\right) = 2 \tan^{-1} x$ for $|x| \leq 1$.

For $x \gt 1$, let $x = \tan \theta$ where $\theta \in (\pi/4, \pi/2)$. Then $\dfrac{2x}{1+x^2} = \sin(2\theta)$. Since $2\theta \in (\pi/2, \pi)$, $\sin^{-1}(\sin(2\theta)) = \pi - 2\theta = \pi - 2\tan^{-1} x$. Thus, the identity does not hold for $x \gt 1$.

For $x \lt -1$, let $x = \tan \theta$ where $\theta \in (-\pi/2, -\pi/4)$. Then $2\theta \in (-\pi, -\pi/2)$. $\sin^{-1}(\sin(2\theta)) = -\pi - 2\theta = -\pi - 2\tan^{-1} x$. Thus, the identity does not hold for $x \lt -1$.

Therefore, the equation holds true if and only if $|x| \leq 1$.

Answer: $|x| \leq 1$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
The principal value branch of $\sin^{-1}(x)$ is $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$. For $\sin^{-1}(\sin(7\pi/5))$, we write $7\pi/5 = \pi + 2\pi/5$. Thus, $\sin(7\pi/5) = \sin(\pi + 2\pi/5) = -\sin(2\pi/5) = \sin(-2\pi/5)$. Since $-2\pi/5 \in [-\pi/2, \pi/2]$, the value is $-2\pi/5$.

The principal value branch of $\sec^{-1}(x)$ is $[0, \pi] \setminus \{\pi/2\}$. For $\sec^{-1}(\sec(7\pi/5))$, we have $7\pi/5 = 2\pi - 3\pi/5$, so $\sec(7\pi/5) = \sec(3\pi/5)$. Since $3\pi/5 \in [0, \pi]$, the value is $3\pi/5$.

The principal value branch of $\tan^{-1}(x)$ is $(-\pi/2, \pi/2)$. For $\tan^{-1}(\tan(7\pi/5))$, we have $7\pi/5 = \pi + 2\pi/5$, so $\tan(7\pi/5) = \tan(2\pi/5)$. Since $2\pi/5 \in (-\pi/2, \pi/2)$, the value is $2\pi/5$.

The principal value branch of $\cos^{-1}(x)$ is $[0, \pi]$. For $\cos^{-1}(\cos(7\pi/5))$, we have $7\pi/5 = 2\pi - 3\pi/5$, so $\cos(7\pi/5) = \cos(3\pi/5)$. Since $3\pi/5 \in [0, \pi]$, the value is $3\pi/5$.

Comparing the results, only $\sin^{-1}(\sin(7\pi/5))$ yields $-2\pi/5$.

Answer: $\sin ^{-1}\left[\sin \left(\dfrac{7 \pi}{5}\right)\right]$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
The expression is $E = \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\right) + \tan^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\right) + \sec^{-1}(2) + \cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) - \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)$.

Simplify each term:
1. $\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\right) = -\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\right) = -\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.
2. $\tan^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) = -\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) = -\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.
3. $\sec^{-1}(2) = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$.
4. $\cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \pi - \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.
5. $\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

Summing these values:
$E = -\dfrac{\pi}{3} - \dfrac{\pi}{6} + \dfrac{\pi}{3} + \dfrac{2\pi}{3} - \dfrac{\pi}{4}$

$E = -\dfrac{\pi}{6} + \dfrac{2\pi}{3} - \dfrac{\pi}{4}$

Finding a common denominator of 12:
$E = \dfrac{-2\pi + 8\pi - 3\pi}{12} = \dfrac{3\pi}{12} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
The expression for $\alpha$ is given by $\alpha = \tan^{-1}(\tan \dfrac{5\pi}{4})$. Since $\dfrac{5\pi}{4}$ is in the third quadrant, $\tan \dfrac{5\pi}{4} = \tan(\pi + \dfrac{\pi}{4}) = \tan \dfrac{\pi}{4} = 1$.

Thus, $\alpha = \tan^{-1}(1) = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

The expression for $\beta$ is given by $\beta = \tan^{-1}(-\tan \dfrac{2\pi}{3})$. Since $\tan \dfrac{2\pi}{3} = \tan(\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3}) = -\tan \dfrac{\pi}{3} = -\sqrt{3}$, we have $-\tan \dfrac{2\pi}{3} = \sqrt{3}$.

Thus, $\beta = \tan^{-1}(\sqrt{3}) = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

Checking the options:

Option (1): $\alpha + \beta = \dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{7\pi}{12} \neq -\dfrac{7\pi}{12}$.

Option (2): $3\alpha = 3(\dfrac{\pi}{4}) = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ and $4\beta = 4(\dfrac{\pi}{3}) = \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$. These are not equal.

Option (3): $\alpha - \beta = \dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = -\dfrac{\pi}{12} \neq \dfrac{7\pi}{12}$.

Option (4): $4\alpha = 4(\dfrac{\pi}{4}) = \pi$ and $3\beta = 3(\dfrac{\pi}{3}) = \pi$. Since $4\alpha = 3\beta = \pi$, this option is correct.

Answer: $4 \alpha=3 \beta$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
The given expression is $E = \cot ^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{3}}\right) - \sec ^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{2}}\right) - \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(-1) - \tan ^{-1}(1)$.

Simplify the arguments:
$\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{3}} = \sqrt{3}$ and $\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{2}$.

Evaluate each term individually:
1. $\cot ^{-1}(-\sqrt{3}) = \pi - \cot ^{-1}(\sqrt{3}) = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$.

2. $\sec ^{-1}(-\sqrt{2}) = \pi - \sec ^{-1}(\sqrt{2}) = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$.

3. $\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(-1) = -\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(1) = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

4. $\tan ^{-1}(1) = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

Substitute these values into the expression $E$:
$E = \dfrac{5\pi}{6} - \dfrac{3\pi}{4} - \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) - \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

Combine the terms:
$E = \dfrac{5\pi}{6} - \dfrac{3\pi}{4} + \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{5\pi}{6} - \pi + \dfrac{\pi}{2} = \dfrac{5\pi - 6\pi + 3\pi}{6} = \dfrac{2\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
The expression is $\cos ^{-1}\left(\cos \dfrac{35 \pi}{18}\right)-\sin ^{-1}\left(\sin \dfrac{35 \pi}{18}\right)$.

First, simplify the argument $\dfrac{35 \pi}{18}$ as $2\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{18}$.

For the cosine term: $\cos ^{-1}\left(\cos \left(2\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{18}\right)\right) = \cos ^{-1}\left(\cos \dfrac{\pi}{18}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{18}$, since $\dfrac{\pi}{18} \in [0, \pi]$.

For the sine term: $\sin ^{-1}\left(\sin \left(2\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{18}\right)\right) = \sin ^{-1}\left(\sin \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{18}\right)\right) = -\dfrac{\pi}{18}$, since $-\dfrac{\pi}{18} \in [-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}]$.

Substituting these values back into the expression:

$\dfrac{\pi}{18} - \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{18}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{18} + \dfrac{\pi}{18} = \dfrac{2\pi}{18} = \dfrac{\pi}{9}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{\pi}{9}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
The expression is $E = \cos^{-1}(\cos(-680^{\circ})) + \sin^{-1}(\sin(-600^{\circ})) - \cos^{-1}(\sin 270^{\circ})$.

First, simplify the angles:
$\cos(-680^{\circ}) = \cos(680^{\circ}) = \cos(720^{\circ} - 40^{\circ}) = \cos(-40^{\circ}) = \cos(40^{\circ})$.
Since $40^{\circ} \in [0, 180^{\circ}]$, $\cos^{-1}(\cos 40^{\circ}) = 40^{\circ}$.

Next, $\sin(-600^{\circ}) = -\sin(600^{\circ}) = -\sin(720^{\circ} - 120^{\circ}) = -(-\sin 120^{\circ}) = \sin 120^{\circ} = \sin(180^{\circ} - 60^{\circ}) = \sin 60^{\circ}$.
Since $60^{\circ} \in [-\pi/2, \pi/2]$, $\sin^{-1}(\sin 60^{\circ}) = 60^{\circ}$.

Finally, $\sin 270^{\circ} = -1$.
$\cos^{-1}(-1) = 180^{\circ}$.

Substituting these values into the expression:
$E = 40^{\circ} + 60^{\circ} - 180^{\circ} = 100^{\circ} - 180^{\circ} = -80^{\circ}$.

Convert $-80^{\circ}$ to radians:
$-80 \times \dfrac{\pi}{180} = -\dfrac{8\pi}{18} = -\dfrac{4\pi}{9}$.

Answer: $-\dfrac{4 \pi}{9}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let the expression inside the cotangent be $\theta$.

$\theta = \dfrac{1}{2} \tan^{-1} \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) + \cos^{-1} \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{12}}{4}\right) + \sin^{-1} \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$

We know that $\tan^{-1} \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

Also, $\dfrac{\sqrt{12}}{4} = \dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{4} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, so $\cos^{-1} \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

And $\sin^{-1} \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

Substituting these values into $\theta$:

$\theta = \dfrac{1}{2} \left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) + \dfrac{\pi}{6} + \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{\pi}{12} + \dfrac{\pi}{6} + \dfrac{\pi}{4}$

Finding a common denominator of 12:

$\theta = \dfrac{\pi + 2\pi + 3\pi}{12} = \dfrac{6\pi}{12} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

The expression becomes $\sin^{-1} [\cot(\theta)] = \sin^{-1} [\cot(\pi/2)]$.

Since $\cot(\pi/2) = 0$, we have $\sin^{-1}(0) = 0$.

Answer: 0

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
The given expression is $\sin^{-1}\left[\cos\left(39 \dfrac{\pi}{5}\right)\right]$.

First, simplify the angle $39 \dfrac{\pi}{5}$ by dividing by $2\pi$:
$39 \dfrac{\pi}{5} = 7\pi + 4 \dfrac{\pi}{5} = 8\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{5}$.

Using the periodicity of the cosine function, $\cos(8\pi - \theta) = \cos(\theta)$, so:
$\cos\left(39 \dfrac{\pi}{5}\right) = \cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{5}\right) = \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{5}\right)$.

Now, rewrite the cosine term as a sine term using the identity $\cos(\theta) = \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right)$:
$\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{5}\right) = \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{\pi}{5}\right) = \sin\left(\dfrac{5\pi - 2\pi}{10}\right) = \sin\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{10}\right)$.

Substituting this back into the original expression:
$\sin^{-1}\left[\sin\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{10}\right)\right]$.

Since $\dfrac{3\pi}{10}$ lies within the principal value range of $\sin^{-1}(x)$, which is $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$, the expression simplifies to $\dfrac{3\pi}{10}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{3 \pi}{10}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: $\text { Let } f(x)=\cos ^{-1}(3 x-1) \text {, then domain of } f(x) \text { is equal to }$
questions.solution:
The function $f(x) = \cos^{-1}(3x - 1)$ is defined when the argument of the inverse cosine function lies in the interval $[-1, 1]$.

Therefore, we set the inequality:

$-1 \le 3x - 1 \le 1$

Adding $1$ to all parts of the inequality:

$-1 + 1 \le 3x - 1 + 1 \le 1 + 1$

$0 \le 3x \le 2$

Dividing by $3$ throughout:

$0 \le x \le \dfrac{2}{3}$

Thus, the domain of $f(x)$ is $[0, \dfrac{2}{3}]$.

Answer: $\left[0, \dfrac{2}{3}\right]$

questions.solution:
We have
$\sin \left[\cot ^{-1}\left\{\cos \left(\tan ^{-1} x\right)\right\}\right]$
Now, $\cos \left(\tan ^{-1} x\right)=\cos \left[\cos ^{-1} \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2}+1}}\right]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2}+1}}\left[\because \cos \left(\cos ^{-1} x\right)=x, \forall x \in[-1,1]\right]$
So, $\cot ^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2}+1}}\right)=\sin ^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{x^{2}+1}}{\sqrt{x^{2}+2}}\right)$
Thus, $\sin \left[\cot ^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2}+1}}\right)\right]=\sin \left[\sin ^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{x^{2}+1}}{\sqrt{x^{2}+2}}\right)\right]=\frac{\sqrt{\left(x^{2}+1\right)}}{\sqrt{x^{2}+2}} \quad\left[\because \sin \left(\sin ^{-1} x\right)=x, \forall x \in[-1,1]\right.$

questions.q: If in a $\triangle A B C, \angle C=\frac{\pi}{2}$, then $\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{a}{b+c}\right)+\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{b}{c+a}\right)=$

Given, $\angle C=\frac{\pi}{2} \Rightarrow c^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}$ \{by pythagoras $\}$ Now, $\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{a}{b+c}\right)+\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{b}{c+a}\right)=\tan ^{-1}\left[\frac{\frac{a}{b+c}+\frac{b}{c+a}}{1-\left(\frac{a}{b+c}\right)\left(\frac{b}{c+a}\right)}\right]=\tan ^{-1}\left[\frac{a c+a^{2}+b^{2}+b c}{b c+b a+c^{2}+c a-a b}\right)$

questions.q: If $\cos ^{-1} x=\alpha,(0 \lt  x \lt  1)$ and $\sin ^{-1}\left(2 x \sqrt{1-x^{2}}\right)+\sec ^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{2 x^{2}-1}\right)=\frac{2 \pi}{3}$, then $\tan ^{-1}(2 x)=$
questions.solution:
Given that, $\cos ^{-1} x=\alpha,(0 \lt  x \lt  1)...(i)\Rightarrow \quad x=\cos \alpha$
Thus, $\sin ^{-1}\left(2 x \sqrt{1-x^{2}}\right)+\sec ^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{2 x^{2}-1}\right)=\frac{2 \pi}{3}\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \sin ^{-1}\left(2 \cos \alpha \sqrt{\left.1-\cos ^{2} \alpha\right)}\right.\\ &+\sec ^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{2 \cos ^{2} \alpha-1}\right)=\frac{2 \pi}{3} \end{aligned}\begin{aligned}
&\Rightarrow \sin ^{-1}(\sin 2 \alpha)+\sec ^{-1}(\sec 2 \alpha)=\frac{2 \pi}{3} \\
&\Rightarrow 2 \alpha+2 \alpha=\frac{2 \pi}{3} \Rightarrow \alpha=\frac{\pi}{6}
\end{aligned}$
Now,$x=\cos \frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \Rightarrow 2 x=\sqrt{3}$
Therefore, $\tan ^{-1}(2 x)=\tan ^{-1} \sqrt{3}=\frac{\pi}{3}$

questions.q: If $a\gt b\gt 0$, then the value of $\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)+\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{a+b}{a-b}\right)$ depends on
questions.solution:
We have,
$\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)+\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{a+b}{a-b}\right)=\tan ^{-1}\left[\frac{\frac{a}{b}+\frac{a+b}{a-b}}{1-\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)\left(\frac{a+b}{a-b}\right)}\right]=\tan ^{-1}\left[\frac{\frac{a^{2}-a b+a b+b^{2}}{b(a-b)}}{\frac{b(a-b)-a(a+b)}{b(a-b)}}\right]=\tan ^{-1}\left[\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}}{a b-b^{2}-a^{2}-a b}\right]=\tan ^{-1}\left[\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}}{-\left(a^{2}+b^{2}\right)}\right]=\tan ^{-1}(-1)$
It does not depends neither $a$ nor $b$.

questions.q: If $\cot ^{-1} \frac{1}{5}+\cot ^{-1} \frac{1}{3}-\cot ^{-1} \frac{4}{7}=\cot ^{-1} x$, then $x$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given, equation is

\begin{aligned}
&\cot ^{-1} \frac{1}{5}+\cot ^{-1} \frac{1}{3}-\cot ^{-1} \frac{4}{7}=\cot ^{-1} x \\
&\Rightarrow \tan ^{-1} 5+\left(\tan ^{-1} 3-\tan ^{-1} \frac{7}{4}\right)=\tan ^{-1} \frac{1}{x} \\
&\Rightarrow \tan ^{-1} 5+\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{3-\frac{7}{4}}{1+3 \times \frac{7}{4}}\right)=\tan ^{-1} \frac{1}{x} \\
&\Rightarrow \tan ^{-1} 5+\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)=\tan ^{-1} \frac{1}{x} \\
&\Rightarrow \tan ^{-1} 5+\cot ^{-1} 5=\tan ^{-1} \frac{1}{x} \\
&\Rightarrow \tan ^{-1} \frac{1}{x}=\frac{\pi}{2} \\
&\Rightarrow \frac{1}{x} \tan {\frac{\pi}{2}}=\tan ^{2} \Rightarrow x=0
\end{aligned}

questions.q: If $\cos ^{-1} p+\cos ^{-1} q+\cos ^{-1} r=\pi$, then $p^{2}+q^{2}+r^{2}+2 p q r$ is equal to
questions.solution:
We have,

\begin{aligned}
&=\cos ^{-1} p+\cos ^{-1} q+\cos ^{-1} r=\pi \\
\Rightarrow & \cos ^{-1} p+\cos ^{-1} q=\pi-\cos ^{-1} r \\
\Rightarrow & \cos ^{-1}\left(p q-\sqrt{1-p^{2}} \sqrt{1-q^{2}}\right)=\pi-\cos ^{-1} r \\
\Rightarrow & p q-\sqrt{1-p^{2}} \sqrt{1-q^{2}}=\cos \left(\pi-\cos ^{-1} r\right) \\
\Rightarrow & p q-\sqrt{1-p^{2}} \sqrt{1-q^{2}}=-\cos \left(\cos ^{-1} r\right) \\
\Rightarrow & p q-\sqrt{1-p^{2}} \sqrt{1-q^{2}}=-r \\
\Rightarrow & p q+r=\sqrt{1-p^{2}} \sqrt{1-q^{2}} \\
\Rightarrow &(p q+r)^{2}=\left(1-p^{2}\right)\left(1-q^{2}\right)
\end{aligned}

$\Rightarrow p^{2} q^{2}+r^{2}+2 p q r=1-p^{2}-q^{2}+p^{2} q^{2}\Rightarrow p^{2}+q^{2}+r^{2}+2 p q r=1$
